candidates.label: Banias (Paneas)
candidates.support: Banias preserves the ancient name Paneas, which Pleiades records together with Caesarea Philippi as alternate names for this single settlement at the southwest foot of Mount Hermon.

summary.text: Caesarea Philippi was a city at the southwest foot of Mount Hermon, near the principal spring source of the Jordan River. In antiquity it was known both as Paneas and as Caesarea Philippi. It is the setting for Peter's confession of Jesus as the Christ.

history.text: Herod Philip built Caesarea at Paneas, in his tetrarchy. When Philip died in the twentieth year of Tiberius (about AD 34), Tiberius added his territory to the province of Syria, and the Roman emperor Caligula then made Herod Agrippa I its king. After Agrippa I's death in AD 44, Claudius sent Cuspius Fadus 'to be procurator of Judea, and of the entire kingdom,' and he gave 'the tetrarchy of Philip and Batanea' to Agrippa II only in AD 53. This project therefore places Caesarea Philippi in the Roman province of Judea for about AD 50.

scripture.textWEB: Now when Jesus came into the parts of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, saying, “Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am?”
Jesus went out, with his disciples, into the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked his disciples, “Who do men say that I am?”

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
politicalHistory.note: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915): "The country of Zenodorus, lying between Trachonitis and Galilee, and including Paneas and Ulatha, Augustus bestowed on Herod" in 20 BC.

Roman province of Syria (ruler: Governor of Syria)
Kingdom of Herod Agrippa I (ruler: Herod Agrippa I)
Roman province of Judea (ruler: Procurators, during Agrippa II's minority)
Kingdom of Herod Agrippa II (ruler: Herod Agrippa II)
politicalHistory.note: Some historians instead place Agrippa II's death, and so the end of this period, before AD 93, reading the Jewish historian Josephus's own wording in the Antiquities; this is the view of, among others, the standard reference work The History of the Jewish People in the Age of Jesus Christ as revised by Vermes and Millar (1973). This area follows the later, AD 100 dating; see that stop for the sources on both sides.

The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) states that Trachonitis "was incorporated in the new province of Arabia" in 106, together with the Nabataean kingdom. No source gives an end point for the other three districts (Gaulanitis, Batanea and Auranitis), so the same year is shown for all four.
